samples.summary: New path-segment redaction misses the workspace invite token (`POST /invites/:token/accept`), which is logged verbatim
samples.evidence: `SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS` (log-safe-url.ts:79) lists exactly one shape: `['share-links','*','resolve']`. But `packages/backend/src/workspace/workspace.controller.ts:117` exposes `POST invites/:token/accept`, where the path segment IS the credential — holding it lets any authenticated account join the workspace. `logSafeUrl` leaves that path untouched (it is not under `/auth`, and no rule matches), so the pino `req` serializer wired in at `app.module.ts:70` writes the live invite token into the access log. Worse than the share-link case the change fixed: `customLogLevel` (app.module.ts:49-60) logs non-GET mutations at `info` (so *successful* accepts too) and any 4xx at `warn` (an expired/revoked/already-a-member attempt), so both the working and the failing token land in the log. Attack: anyone with read access to the access log (operators, log shippers, an agent harness transcript) lifts a still-valid invite token and accepts it into a workspace they were never invited to. This is exactly the class of gap the change's own commentary claims to have closed ("grep for the credential's *other* carriers before calling it covered").

samples.summary: `JWT_SECRET` is reused as the OAuth-state HMAC key, and one unauthenticated request hands an attacker a chosen-free (input, HMAC) pair for it
samples.evidence: `bindingSecret()` (line 176) returns `JWT_SECRET` — the same key `AuthModule`'s `JwtModule` signs and verifies session/refresh JWTs with (`auth.module.ts:19`) — and `stateSignature()` (line 195) publishes `HMAC-SHA256(JWT_SECRET, cookieValue)` as the `state` query parameter, while the *input* (`cookieValue`) is returned to the same caller in `Set-Cookie` by the same response (guard lines 359-365). So an unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` yields a verified plaintext/MAC pair under the JWT signing key. That is an offline brute-force oracle for `JWT_SECRET`: with a weak or guessable secret an attacker recovers it without ever creating an account or capturing a JWT, and then forges access tokens for any `sub` (full account takeover). Key separation is the fix (derive a distinct key, e.g. HKDF over `JWT_SECRET` with a `oauth-state` label, or a dedicated env var). The file's own comment argues at length about what the signature does and does not buy but never addresses the key reuse.

samples.summary: The CLI consent token authorizes *any* CLI parameters — it is not bound to the port/nonce/challenge the page displayed
samples.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` (line 342) mints a bare 32-byte random value with no association to the `port`, `nonce` or `code_challenge` of the consent request, and `hasConfirmation()` (lines 371-383) only compares the query half to the cookie half. So the gate proves "this browser was shown *some* CLI consent page in the last 5 minutes", not "this browser was shown the page naming port 9876". The whole documented defence is that the person read the port on the page they clicked; a confirm token obtained (or observed) for one set of parameters is spendable against a completely different `port=`, i.e. against an attacker-owned loopback listener, with no second consent page. Any leak of the token — it travels in a URL query string and therefore into browser history, and any future `Referrer-Policy` regression or non-`/auth` route prefix would put it in the access log — converts directly into the exact attack the interstitial exists to stop. I could not construct an end-to-end leak on the current code (the cookie is httpOnly, the page sets `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">`, and `logSafeUrl` redacts `/auth` query strings), hence low confidence; the fix is cheap: HMAC the consent parameters into the token, or store `{token -> {port,nonce,codeChallenge}}` and require them to match on the confirmed request.

samples.summary: A repeated `?state=` query parameter makes the callback throw a raw TypeError (500) instead of failing closed with the documented refusal
samples.evidence: `@Query('state') stateToken: string | undefined` (line 216) is not validated — the global `ValidationPipe` (main.ts:65) does not apply to a scalar `@Query()` binding — and Express turns `?state=a&state=b` into an array. `verifyCallbackState` then calls `stateToken?.startsWith(WEB_STATE_PREFIX)` (line 293); arrays have no `startsWith`, so a `TypeError` is thrown. The `catch` at line 223 only converts `UnauthorizedException`, so the TypeError is rethrown and rendered as a 500. No session is issued, so this is not an auth bypass, but it is an unauthenticated 500 on the OAuth callback (and it defeats the change's stated invariant that a callback with a bad `state` lands on `/login?error=login_state`). Guard with `typeof stateToken === 'string'` before use.

samples.summary: `ERROR_MESSAGES[error]` is an unguarded prototype-chain lookup on an attacker-supplied query value, crashing the login page
samples.evidence: `error` comes straight from `searchParams.get("error")` (line 28) and is used as an object index at line 48 with only `?? FALLBACK_ERROR` as a guard. `?error=__proto__` resolves to `Object.prototype` (an object, not undefined, so the `??` never fires) and React throws "Objects are not valid as a React child"; `?error=constructor` / `?error=toString` resolve to functions. A crafted link therefore blanks or error-boundaries the sign-in page for any visitor — a low-effort denial of the login route, and the URL is exactly the shape users are now sent (`FRONTEND_URL/login?error=…`). Use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(ERROR_MESSAGES, error)` or a `Map`.

samples.summary: `GET /auth/github` unconditionally rotates the browser state cookie, so any cross-site page can break an in-flight login
samples.evidence: Every unauthenticated `GET /auth/github` reaches line 359-365 and issues a fresh `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie at `Path=/`. A third-party page firing `` (or a no-cors fetch) gets that `Set-Cookie` stored in the victim's jar — `SameSite=Lax` restricts when a cookie is *sent*, not when it is *set* — overwriting the value the victim's genuine pending login is bound to. Their GitHub callback then fails `secretEquals` in `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:303) and they are bounced to `/login?error=login_state`, repeatable indefinitely. Not a credential compromise (the attacker never learns or chooses the planted value), but it is a remotely triggerable denial of the sign-in flow that the separate-cookie-name reasoning in this same change was written to avoid for the CLI/browser pair. Consider keying the state cookie per in-flight login (e.g. a name suffix carried in `state`) so a second start cannot clobber the first.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` holds a live login URL and is only removed on the normal path, so an interrupted login leaves it on disk
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` writes the full authorization URL — nonce plus PKCE challenge, described in the same file as "one-time login secrets" — to `~/.wafflebase/login-url.txt` (line 227). It is deleted only in the `finally` around `waitForCallback` (line 81), which never runs if the process is killed (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, a crash before that block), leaving a credential file behind for the remaining 5 minutes of the server-side TTL and, in practice, indefinitely. The file mode is `0600`, but `mkdirSync(dirname(file), {recursive:true})` (line 223) creates the directory with the default `0755`, so the path is discoverable. Also note `getConfigPath()` honours `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG`, so the directory is not necessarily under `$HOME`. A process-exit handler (or writing to a `mkdtemp` dir with `0700`) would close the gap.

samples.summary: `loopbackCallback` exempts the CLI login from the https requirement based on the *callback* host, which need not be the origin the user's browser sees
samples.evidence: `cliLoginAvailable` (line 119) waives the new plain-http refusal whenever `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s host is `localhost`/`127.0.0.0/8`. That is the URL GitHub redirects to, which on a proxied or port-forwarded install is not the origin the victim's browser uses; a deployment configured with `http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback` but reached by users at `http://intranet.corp/` would run the whole CLI consent gate behind an unprefixed, plantable cookie while the guard believes it is on loopback. The justification in the comment ("planting a cookie on http://localhost already means running code on the machine the terminal is on") only holds when the *browser's* origin is loopback, which this predicate does not establish. Low confidence because the configuration is unusual, but the check is the only thing separating "gate enforced" from "gate anyone on the origin can open".

samples.summary: Request-derived `req.path` is interpolated into the consent page's `href` with only HTML escaping
samples.evidence: `renderCliConsent(consent, req.path || '/auth/github')` (line 144) uses the raw request path as the link target. It is HTML-escaped (line 172), and Express's router matches the raw pathname against `/^\/auth\/github\/?$/i`, so today the value can only be a case/trailing-slash variant of `/auth/github` and no scheme-relative or absolute URL can reach it. Flagged only because the safety rests entirely on router-matching behaviour that a future global prefix, mount point, or router option could change, at which point the Continue link becomes attacker-influenced. Pinning the literal route (or validating that `self` starts with a single `/`) removes the dependency.

verdict.reason: Verified independently. log-safe-url.ts:75-79 defines SECRET_PATH_SEGMENTS with exactly one rule (['share-links','*','resolve']); redactPathSecrets (82-105) requires an exact segment-count and literal match and otherwise returns the path unchanged, and isAuthPath (12-23) only covers /auth. workspace.controller.ts:117 exposes POST invites/:token/accept, and workspace.service.ts:152-178 resolves the invite by token alone (no email/identity binding), creating a workspaceMember for whichever authenticated user presents it; schema.prisma:153 shows token is a unique uuid bearer credential. app.module.ts:66-73 pipes req.url through logSafeUrl into the access log, customLogLevel (49-61) emits info for non-GET mutations and warn for any 4xx, and /invites is not in the images/cells debug carve-out; redact.paths (78-85) covers only headers. I searched wide for a counterexample: a repo-wide grep for logSafeUrl|setGlobalPrefix|pinoHttp|serializers|redact shows exactly one logger config and one call site with no URL-rewriting middleware, and log-safe-url.spec.ts contains no invite case. The token also rides in the path from the real frontend client (packages/frontend/src/api/workspaces.ts:156), so this is the live shape. In-lane as logged-credential / sensitive data exposure: a log reader lifts a still-valid invite token and joins a workspace uninvited.

verdict.reason: The described code exists exactly as claimed and is reachable unauthenticated. `bindingSecret()` (github-auth.guard.ts:175-177) returns `JWT_SECRET`, the same key `JwtModule` (auth.module.ts:16-26) and `AuthService` (auth.service.ts:51-53, 98-119) use to sign/verify access, refresh and Yorkie tokens. `stateSignature()` (github-auth.guard.ts:195-197) HMAC-SHA256s the random cookie value under that key, and `canActivate` (github-auth.guard.ts:359-365) emits both halves in one response: the cookie value via `issueLoginCookie`'s `res.cookie` (lines 402-405) and its tag as the OAuth `state`, forwarded into the redirect `Location` by `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` (github.strategy.ts:61-68). The route `GET /auth/github` carries only `GitHubAuthGuard`, no authentication (auth.controller.ts:111-113), so any anonymous caller obtains a verified plaintext/MAC pair under the JWT signing key — an offline brute-force oracle against a weak `JWT_SECRET`, with no minimum-entropy validation anywhere (only presence via `requireConfig`). No guard elsewhere makes this unreachable, and cross-context key reuse for crypto is squarely in the security lens (crypto/auth). Severity as a clear crypto weakness (major) is appropriate; blocking under the rubric.

verdict.reason: The claimed code is present verbatim. `issueLoginCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:393-407) returns a bare `randomBytes(32)` value with no input from `portNum`, `nonce` or `codeChallenge`, even though all three are in scope at the call site (github-auth.guard.ts:338-343). `hasConfirmation` (github-auth.guard.ts:371-383) compares only the `cli_confirm` query value against the cookie, so a live token/cookie pair satisfies the gate for ANY parameter triple: the interstitial branch at line 337 is skipped and `cliAuthStore.createState` (349-355) is called with attacker-chosen `port`, which the callback then uses to redirect the authorization code to `http://127.0.0.1:${port}` (auth.controller.ts:249-261) with no second consent page. The token does travel in a URL query string (auth.controller.ts:165-172). The mitigations that exist — httpOnly/`__Host-` cookies (github-auth.guard.ts:138-157), `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">` (auth.controller.ts:180), `Cache-Control: no-store` and frame-ancestors (auth.controller.ts:137-141), `logSafeUrl` redaction of `/auth` query strings (logging/log-safe-url.spec.ts:15-35), and single-use clearing (github-auth.guard.ts:348) — lower the chance of a token leak but none of them binds the token to the consent parameters, so they do not make the described path unreachable; they are ambient controls, not a guard on this gate. No named refutation ground applies: the code is present, unguarded with respect to parameter binding, and consent/auth binding is squarely in the security lane, where the rubric rates a clear weakness short of a full exploit as major.

finding.summary: On a non-HTTPS deployment the `wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookie loses its `__Host-` prefix, so anyone who can plant a cookie on the origin can forge the human confirmation the new headers exist to protect
finding.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` names the cookie via `loginCookieName` (github-auth.guard.ts:92-97), which only adds `__Host-` when `secureCookies()` is true (line 71-75: NODE_ENV=production or an https `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`). On any plain-http deployment the wire name is the bare `wafflebase_cli_confirm`, an ordinary host cookie. An attacker who can write the victim's cookie jar for that origin (sibling subdomain, or a network position on cleartext http) sets `wafflebase_cli_confirm=X` and then sends the victim a single link `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker listener>&nonce=…&code_challenge=…&cli_confirm=X`. `hasConfirmation` (line 313-325) compares the query half against the cookie half and both are the attacker's, so the guard skips the interstitial entirely, mints the state and redirects straight to GitHub — the consent page the victim never sees, and the code is delivered to the attacker's loopback port. The delta hardens that page against click theft while the click itself remains skippable on these deployments. Note the same `__Host-` caveat is documented for the *state* cookie (loginCookieName's comment) but not for the confirm cookie, whose whole value is being unforgeable from a link.

verdict.reason: The claimed bypass requires a plain-http, non-loopback deployment, but `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` refuses exactly that case before any confirm-cookie logic runs: `github-auth.guard.ts:297-301` throws `BadRequestException('Command-line sign-in requires an https server')` when `cliLoginAvailable()` is false, and `cliLoginAvailable` (119-121) is `secureCookies() || loopbackCallback()`, with `loopbackCallback` (85-98) accepting only localhost/[::1]/127.0.0.0/8 and returning false for an unset or unparseable callback URL. `hasConfirmation` (337, 371-383) is never reached on such an origin, so the attacker's planted `wafflebase_cli_confirm` cookie plus `cli_confirm=` link cannot skip the interstitial there. The only deployments where the bare (non-`__Host-`) confirm cookie name is in play are loopback ones, where planting a cookie already implies local code execution on the same machine the code would be delivered to — an exception explicitly reasoned about at 112-117. The NODE_ENV=production-over-http variant is not a bypass either: `hasConfirmation` reads the `__Host-`-prefixed name with `secure: true` (142, 153), which a non-secure origin cannot set — that yields a broken login, not a forgeable one. No other call site reaches CLI state minting (`cliAuthStore.createState` is called only at github-auth.guard.ts:349 outside specs). The refusal is pinned by github-auth.guard.spec.ts:307-317, which feeds a fully forged cookie+query pair on an http non-loopback config and asserts a BadRequestException with no state, no consent page, and no cookies issued.
